On 10 April 1912 the RMS Titanic left Southampton, England, on its first voyage.
It was going to New York.
Many people believed that the huge new ship was unsinkable, because four of its sixteen watertight compartments could flood without danger.
Shortly before midnight on 14 April the ship hit an iceberg in the North Atlantic, south-east of Newfoundland.
Water started to come in, and on 15 April the Titanic sank.
About 2,200 people were on board, but the lifeboats had places for only 1,178 people.
Some 1,500 people died.
For many years nobody knew where exactly the wreck was.
Finally, in 1985, a team led by Robert Ballard found it at a depth of about 4,000 meters.
The ship lay in two pieces.
Wilbur and Orville Wright were two brothers from Dayton, Ohio.
In 1892 they opened a bicycle shop, the Wright Cycle Company.
The money from the shop paid for their experiments with flying.
First they built kites and gliders.
In 1903 they took their airplane, the Wright Flyer, to Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk in North Carolina.
The steady winds there helped the plane to get into the air.
The brothers tossed a coin to decide who would fly first.
Wilbur won, but his attempt on 14 December failed.
Three days later, on 17 December 1903, it was Orville's turn.
He flew for 12 seconds and covered about 37 meters (120 feet).
It was the first powered, controlled flight with a pilot.
That day the brothers made four flights.
The last one, with Wilbur, lasted 59 seconds and covered about 260 meters.
Many Americans learn that the "first Thanksgiving" took place in 1621.
But what do we really know?
In 1621 the English colonists at Plymouth, often called the Pilgrims, celebrated their first harvest.
One colonist, Edward Winslow, described it in a letter.
He wrote that the Wampanoag leader Massasoit came with about 90 men and that they feasted together for three days.
The Wampanoag brought five deer, and the colonists hunted birds.
However, Winslow did not use the word "Thanksgiving", and he did not mention turkey.
The name "the first Thanksgiving" came much later.
The popular picture of a peaceful turkey dinner is mostly tradition, not history.
In 1863, after a long campaign by Sarah Josepha Hale, President Abraham Lincoln made Thanksgiving a national holiday.
Today some Native Americans mark the day as a "National Day of Mourning".
Ada Lovelace was born in London on 10 December 1815.
Her father was the famous poet Lord Byron, but her parents separated when she was only about a month old.
Her mother, Lady Byron, had studied mathematics and made sure that Ada studied it too.
In 1833, when Ada was 17, she met the inventor Charles Babbage at a party.
Later he designed a machine called the Analytical Engine.
Ada was fascinated by his ideas.
In 1843 she translated an article about the machine from French into English.
She added her own notes, which were about three times longer than the article.
In one note she explained how the machine could calculate special numbers called Bernoulli numbers.
Because of this many people call her the first computer programmer, although historians still argue about her exact role.
She also imagined that such machines might one day compose music.
Sadly, she died in 1852, aged only 36.
Apollo 13 left Earth on April 11, 1970.
Its crew were Jim Lovell, Jack Swigert and Fred Haise, and they planned to land on the Moon.
Almost 56 hours after launch an oxygen tank exploded.
Swigert reported the problem, and Lovell repeated: “Houston, we've had a problem”.
The landing was canceled, and the astronauts now had only one goal: to get home alive.
They moved into the lunar module, Aquarius, and used it as a lifeboat.
Soon carbon dioxide began to build up in the air.
Engineers on the ground designed a fix, and the crew built it from plastic covers and duct tape.
The spacecraft flew around the Moon and headed back to Earth.
On April 17 it splashed down safely in the South Pacific.
During the flight the crew went farther from Earth than any humans before them.
That record lasted 56 years, until Artemis II broke it in April 2026.

Silicon Valley is a region in the south of the San Francisco Bay Area in California.
It is named after silicon, the material used in computer chips.
The journalist Don Hoefler made the name popular in 1971.
Before the computer age the area was famous for its fruit orchards, especially apricots and prunes.
People called it “the Valley of Heart's Delight”.
In 1939 Bill Hewlett and David Packard started their company in a garage in Palo Alto with just $538.
Their first product was an audio oscillator, and Walt Disney Studios bought eight of them for the film “Fantasia”.
Today the garage is known as “the Birthplace of Silicon Valley”.
In 1956 William Shockley opened a laboratory to make semiconductors.
A year later eight of his engineers left and founded Fairchild Semiconductor.
In 1968 two of them, Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore, founded the company that became Intel.
In the early 1800s, moving goods from the Atlantic coast to the Great Lakes was slow and expensive.
DeWitt Clinton, who became governor of New York in 1817, strongly supported a bold plan: to dig a canal from the Hudson River to Lake Erie.
Many people laughed at the idea and called it “Clinton's Ditch.” Work began on July 4, 1817, in Rome, New York.
Many of the workers were Irish immigrants.
The canal opened on October 26, 1825.
It was 363 miles long, 40 feet wide and only 4 feet deep, and it had 83 locks.
A lock works like a water step: it raises or lowers a boat.
Mules and horses walked along a path next to the water and pulled the boats.
To celebrate, Clinton traveled by boat to New York City and poured water from Lake Erie into New York Harbor.
People called this “the Wedding of the Waters.” The canal changed the country.
Before it opened, sending a ton of goods from Buffalo to New York City cost about $100 and took about three weeks.
After it opened, it cost less than $10, and the trip became much faster.
New York City gained a big advantage over other American ports.
The Library of Congress in Washington, D.C. is the national library of the United States.
It was founded on April 24, 1800, when President John Adams signed a law that gave $5,000 for books for Congress.
At first the small library was inside the Capitol.
In 1814, during the War of 1812, British troops burned the Capitol, and about 3,000 books were lost.
Former president Thomas Jefferson offered to sell his own library, one of the finest private book collections in the country.
In 1815 Congress paid $23,950 for his 6,487 books.
Sadly, another fire in 1851 destroyed about two-thirds of Jefferson's books.
The collection kept growing.
From 1870 the library had the right to receive two copies of every work protected by copyright in the US.
In 1897 it moved into a beautiful new building, now called the Thomas Jefferson Building.
Today the library has three buildings on Capitol Hill.
In 2023 it held more than 178 million items: books, maps, letters, photographs, films, sheet music and sound recordings in about 470 languages.
Jazz was born in New Orleans, Louisiana, around the turn of the 20th century.
It grew out of the music of African American communities.
Long before jazz, enslaved people gathered on Sundays at a place that later became known as Congo Square, where they played drums and danced.
By the 1890s the city was full of music.
Brass bands played at parades, concerts and dances.
People also loved the blues, spirituals and ragtime, lively piano music.
The cornet player Buddy Bolden added the blues to popular dance tunes and played them faster.
Many early jazz musicians believed that he was the first to play in this new style.
Sadly, no recordings of his music exist.
In 1917 a white band from New Orleans, the Original Dixieland Jass Band, made the first jazz records in New York.
The records became a hit, and jazz spread across the country.
Many musicians from New Orleans moved to Chicago and New York.
One of them was Louis Armstrong, who was born in New Orleans in 1901.
As a boy he learned to play the cornet in a home for boys.
In 1922 his mentor King Oliver invited him to Chicago.
Armstrong's brilliant solos changed jazz forever.
Before 1869 a trip from the East Coast to California could take months.
In 1862, during the Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln signed the Pacific Railway Act.
Two companies began to build a railroad across the country.
The Central Pacific started in Sacramento, California, and built east.
The Union Pacific started near Omaha, Nebraska, and built west.
The Central Pacific had to cut tunnels through the Sierra Nevada.
Most of its workers were immigrants from China: at times they made up about 90 percent of the workforce.
They often did the most dangerous work, such as blasting rock, and were paid less than white workers.
Many died in explosions and avalanches, but nobody knows the exact number.
The Union Pacific hired many Irish immigrants and former Civil War soldiers.
On May 10, 1869, the two lines met at Promontory Summit, Utah Territory.
Leland Stanford, the president of the Central Pacific, tapped a golden spike, and a telegraph sent one word across the country: “Done.” Now people could cross the continent in about a week.
But for many Native American nations the railroad brought hard times: it crossed their lands and helped to destroy the huge bison herds that they depended on for food.
John Muir was born in Dunbar, Scotland, in 1838.
His family moved to Wisconsin in 1849.
In 1867, while he was working in a factory, a tool hit him in the eye.
For six weeks he stayed in a dark room and was afraid that he would go blind.
When he recovered, he decided to spend his life studying nature.
He walked about 1,000 miles from Kentucky to the Gulf coast of Florida.
In 1868 Muir first visited Yosemite in California.
The valley had been home to Native American peoples for thousands of years.
Muir fell in love with its granite cliffs, waterfalls and giant sequoias.
He wrote articles and warned that the wild mountains needed protection.
In 1890 Congress created Yosemite National Park.
Two years later Muir helped to start the Sierra Club and became its first president.
In 1903 President Theodore Roosevelt visited Yosemite, and the two men camped outdoors together.
Muir asked the president to protect the area better.
In 1906 Yosemite Valley became part of the national park.
But Muir lost one of his biggest battles: in 1913 the government approved a dam in the Hetch Hetchy Valley inside the park.
He died a year later, on December 24, 1914.
Today many people call him “the Father of the National Parks.”
Hoover Dam stands on the Colorado River, in Black Canyon, on the border between Nevada and Arizona.
It was built between 1931 and 1936, during the Great Depression.
Millions of Americans had lost their jobs, so thousands of people came to the desert hoping to find work.
At the peak, in 1934, more than 5,000 people worked on the project.
A new town, Boulder City, was built for the workers.
The work was hard and dangerous.
Officially, 96 men died at the dam site from causes such as falls, falling rocks and drowning.
A popular myth says that some workers are buried inside the concrete.
This is not true.
The concrete was poured into blocks a little at a time, and several workers watched every bucket.
The dam is 726 feet (221 meters) high and contains about 3.25 million cubic yards of concrete.
It was finished more than two years ahead of schedule.
President Franklin D.
Roosevelt dedicated it on September 30, 1935.
Behind the dam lies Lake Mead, one of the largest reservoirs in the US.
Its power plant sends electricity to Nevada, Arizona and California.
For a time the dam was officially called Boulder Dam, but in 1947 Congress brought back the name of President Herbert Hoover.

The Statue of Liberty is a gift of friendship from France to the United States.
Its full name is "Liberty Enlightening the World".
The idea came in 1865 from Édouard de Laboulaye, who suggested a statue of liberty for the 100th birthday of the United States.
A young sculptor, Auguste Bartholdi, liked the idea and in 1876 began to build the statue in France.
Inside the statue is an iron framework, which the engineer Gustave Eiffel designed.
It is 98 feet tall.
Outside, the statue is covered with thin copper sheets.
The copper is only 3/32 of an inch, about as thick as two pennies stacked together.
The crown has 25 windows and seven rays.
The tablet shows the date July 4, 1776, written in Roman numerals.
From the ground to the tip of the torch it measures 305 feet, about 93 meters.
Americans had to build the pedestal, which Richard Morris Hunt designed.
In 1884 the money ran out and work stopped.
Then, in 1885, Joseph Pulitzer started a fundraising campaign, which saved the project.
Meanwhile, the statue was taken apart and shipped to New York on the French navy ship "Isère", which arrived on June 17.
The statue waited for a year in storage, until the pedestal was finished.
On October 28, 1886, President Grover Cleveland accepted the statue for the United States.
Earlier, in 1883, Emma Lazarus had given her poem "The New Colossus" to an auction, which raised money for the pedestal.
In 1903 the poem was engraved on a bronze plaque at the base.
Many immigrants saw the raised torch as a sign of welcome.
Since 1933, the National Park Service has cared for the statue.
In the 1980s, a restoration gave it a new torch, covered in gold leaf, and the original is now in the museum on Liberty Island.
